newsitem.title: USA: US Senators offer sliding scale capital gains tax.
newsitem.headline: US Senators offer sliding scale capital gains tax.

text.p: Two Senators Friday proposed an alternative sliding scale approach to capital gains tax cuts, which would give bigger cuts to long-term holdings and halve the rate for assets held at least eight years.

Sen. Judd Gregg, a New Hampshire Republican, and Sen. Wendell Ford, a Kentucky Democrat, said their plan would cut maximum capital gains taxes in half for long-term assets. They said it would help family-owned farms and businesses and encourage savings and long-term investment.
They also said it would cost $45.2 billion over 10 years, instead of the $129 billion foreseen in the original Senate proposal.

Under the overall bipartisan budget agreement, Congress is seeking $250 billion in net tax cuts over 10 years, from capital gains cuts, estate tax relief, a $500 per child tax credit and education tax initiatives.
"This is a better approach," said Ford. "It fits into the tax package that we're going to have to deal with.

For someone in the 28 percent tax bracket, there would be no reduction in the tax rate in the first year, but it would gradually drop two percent a year for each additional year an asset was held. Assets held more than eight years would be taxes at 14 percent versus the current 28 percent rate. Rates would be similarly slashed for higher tax brackets.

Gregg said the approach, which merged two separate proposals each senator had drafted earlier, rewards job-creation and savings over speculation. "We are a quarter-by-quarter society when it comes to investment," Gregg said.
The senators said Finance Committee chairman Sen. William Roth, a Republican from Delaware, had assured them their proposal would be "on the table."
Gregg and Ford both said Clinton administration officials had not made any commitment but seemed to look favorably on the initiative.
